samasa.literal: she whose self is the measures
samasa.sense: she who exists as the three sounds a, u and m of Om

samasa.type: saptamī tatpuruṣa (अर्धमात्रा is itself a tatpuruṣa: मात्रायाः अर्धम् ‘half of a mora’)
samasa.sense: she who is present in the faint resonance that closes Om
samasa.alt: The printed text joins अर्धमात्रास्थिता; it can also be divided as two words, अर्धमात्रा स्थिता ‘(you) abide as the half-mora’, and then या refers to the half-mora. The compound is kept as printed.

morph.note: Gerundive of the causative of उद् + √चर् (उच्चारयति ‘pronounces’): उच्चार्य ‘to be pronounced’; with the negative अन्- ‘not pronounceable’.

Ambiguous form: n. loc. sg. of अक्षर (‘in the imperishable syllable’) or f. voc. sg. of अक्षरा (‘O Imperishable!’). The locative is chosen because it gives स्थिता its place and matches the half-mora of the next line.
The suffix -धा makes adverbs of manner from numerals: त्रिधा ‘in three ways’, बहुधा ‘in many ways’ (1.65).

mantras.anvaya: त्वं सुधा। त्वं नित्ये अक्षरे त्रिधा मात्रात्मिका स्थिता। (त्वं) या विशेषतः अनुच्चार्या, नित्या, अर्धमात्रास्थिता (असि)।
mantras.anvaya_en: A short identity (सुधा त्वम्), a participial predicate with a locative of place, and a second predicate expanded by a relative clause (या … विशेषतः).
mantras.lit: You are nectar; in the eternal imperishable (syllable) you abide threefold, having the morae as your self; you abide in the half-mora, eternal, (you) who cannot be uttered distinctly.
mantras.tr: You are the nectar of immortality. In the eternal, imperishable syllable you dwell as its three sounds; and you dwell in the half-measure beyond them, eternal, which no voice can utter as a separate sound.
mantras.tr_note: ‘Syllable’ and ‘its three sounds’ interpret अक्षर and मात्रा as the syllable Om and its parts a, u, m, the standard sense in this context.

comm.t: The Goddess is identified with the sacred syllable: she abides in its three morae (a, u, m) and in the half-mora — the fading resonance after m — which cannot be pronounced as a distinct sound. She is also सुधा, the nectar of immortality.

The analysis of Om into three measures and a fourth beyond utterance is Upaniṣadic: the Māṇḍūkya Upaniṣad treats a, u and m as the three states of waking, dream and deep sleep and the ‘measureless fourth’ (अमात्रः चतुर्थः) as the self beyond them. Brahmā places the Goddess both in the three and in what lies beyond them.

A modern reading: the hymn begins with words that can be spoken — svāhā, svadhā, vaṣaṭ — and moves at once to the part of the sacred sound that cannot be spoken. Praise here is a way of approaching what speech cannot hold.

flags.uncertain: अक्षरे नित्ये may be locative (‘in the eternal imperishable [syllable]’, chosen here) or two feminine vocatives (‘O Imperishable, O Eternal One’); both are grammatical and both are found in translations. अर्धमात्रास्थिता is printed as one word; a division into अर्धमात्रा स्थिता is equally possible.

Taddhita in -ī from सवितृ: ‘belonging to Savitṛ’, the name of the Gāyatrī verse addressed to the Sun-god Savitṛ.
Feminine agent noun from √जन् with -ana and -ī: ‘she who gives birth’.

mantras.anvaya: त्वम् एव संध्या, सावित्री। देवि, त्वं परा जननी। त्वया एतत् विश्वं धार्यते, त्वया एतत् जगत् सृज्यते।
mantras.anvaya_en: Identity statements (त्वम् … संध्या सावित्री; त्वम् … जननी परा), then two parallel passive sentences with त्वया as agent.
mantras.lit: You alone are Sandhyā and Sāvitrī; you, O Goddess, are the supreme mother. By you this universe is upheld; by you this world is created.
mantras.tr: You alone are the sacred twilight and the Sāvitrī verse; you, O Goddess, are the supreme Mother. By you this universe is sustained, and by you this world is brought forth.

comm.t: Brahmā continues identifying her with the forms of sacred worship — the twilight rite (Sandhyā) and the Sāvitrī verse recited in it — and then names her the supreme Mother, by whom the world is created and sustained.

Sandhyā and Sāvitrī belong together: the Sāvitrī (Gāyatrī) verse addressed to Savitṛ is recited at the twilight worship. To call the Goddess both is to make the daily Vedic observance itself her form. The verse then passes from ritual to cosmology: the one invoked at dawn and dusk is the mother of the world.
Lalitā Sahasranāma (Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa) has 422, सन्ध्या; 699, सावित्री; and 823, जननी.

samasa.sense: you take the form of creation when the world is made
you take the form of preservation while the world endures

morph.note: Present 2nd singular of √अद्, a root-class (adādi) verb: अद् + सि, the d unvoiced to t before s (खरि च, 8.4.55). ‘You eat’ — the image of dissolution as the world swallowed back.
Passive of the curādi root √पाल् (पालयति): the -aya- of the present drops before the passive -ya (पाल्-य-ते).

mantras.anvaya: देवि, त्वया एतत् पाल्यते; अन्ते च सर्वदा त्वम् (एतत्) अत्सि। विसृष्टौ त्वं सृष्टिरूपा, पालने च स्थितिरूपा, …
mantras.anvaya_en: A passive sentence, an active one with an understood object (एतत्), and a series of nominal predicates with locatives of occasion, continued in 1.77 (संहृतिरूपा).
mantras.lit: By you this is protected, O Goddess, and you devour (it) at the end, always. In creation you have the form of creation, and the form of preservation in protecting,
mantras.tr: By you, O Goddess, it is protected, and at the end of every age you consume it. When the world is brought forth, you are its creation; while it is sustained, you are its preservation;
mantras.tr_note: सर्वदा ‘always’ with अन्ते is rendered ‘at the end of every age’: each dissolution, not one alone.

comm.t: The three cosmic works are given to her one after another: she protects the world, consumes it at every end, and in each phase takes the form of that phase — creation in creating, preservation in protecting. Dissolution follows in 1.77.

The three works ordinarily assigned to Brahmā, Viṣṇu and Rudra are all hers; the speaker is Brahmā himself, the creator, who here says that creation is her form. The tradition reads this as the Devī Māhātmya’s central claim: the gods act through her power.
